text.p: Compaq Computer Corp and Gateway 2000 had agreed to an almost $7 billion merger last month, before it was rejected at the last minute by Gateway founder Ted Waitt, Time Magazine reported.
In its May 19 issue, Time reported that contracts for a deal were drawn up but Waitt put a stop to the deal, "possibly hours before it was to be announced."
The computer industry has been rife with rumors for several weeks that the two companies were in merger talks. Both Compaq and Gateway have repeatedly declined to comment.
Gateway officials could not be reached for comment. Compaq officials were also not immediately available for comment.

In an interview late last month, Earl Mason, Compaq's chief financial officer, declined to comment on rumors that Compaq almost merged with Gateway, only to say that Compaq looks at many companies all the time.

He also declined to comment on Micron Electronics Inc's statement last month, confirming that Compaq held early talks with Micron about a merger. Both Gateway and Micron are direct makers of PCs and Compaq is shifting its manufacturing strategy to a similar build-to-order model.
Time Magazine reported that a press release was in the works and that Waitt had dispatched a courier to foreign offices to deliver the news to key executives.
Time reported that the deal appears to have fallen apart when Compaq started to flex its muscle and Waitt realized that he did not want Compaq CEO Eckhard Pfeiffer, or anyone, to be his boss.
Waitt founded Gateway, in North Sioux City, S.D., in 1985 with a $10,000 loan from his grandmother.
